title: Jackson County, CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Jackson County water wells have a 100 ft median depth and 10 gpm median yield. Here’s what that means for drilling cost, water levels, and buying land.
h1: Water wells in Jackson County, Colorado
intro_html: Jackson County wells are classic high-mountain bedrock wells: relatively shallow on average, but in hard fractured rock that can vary from place to place. Looking at all 1,600 permits on record gives a pretty clear picture of what you’re likely to drill into, how much water you’ll get, and what a new well will cost in this part of North Park.

sections.heading: How deep Jackson County wells usually are
sections.html:
Across Jackson County, the median well depth is about 100 feet. The middle half of wells land between 60 and 160 feet, so that’s the range most drillers will have in mind when they price a domestic well here. About 41% of wells are under 100 feet, and another 51% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 7% go 300–600 feet, and just 1% are deeper than 600 feet, even though the single deepest well on record runs down to 3,466 feet.

Almost all of these are in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, which means depth can change quickly over short distances. When you bid a well here, plan for at least the 160-foot upper-middle range, and know there’s a small but real chance your hole needs to go a few hundred feet deeper than that.

sections.heading: Well yields and how much water to expect
sections.html:
On production, Jackson County looks pretty favorable for a mountain county. The median reported yield is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells come in between 7.0 and 15.0 gpm. That’s plenty for a standard exempt household-use well and normal indoor use plus some outdoor watering within your permit limits.

Only about 2% of tested wells report under 1 gpm, and 9% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Most wells, 63%, are in the 5–15 gpm range, and 26% are 15+ gpm. Those numbers suggest the fractured bedrock here tends to have decent water-bearing fractures once you find them, but there is still a small slice of low-yield or finicky wells to be aware of when you buy a property.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they mean for pumping
sections.html:
Static water levels in Jackson County are generally not far below ground, which keeps pumping costs and lift requirements reasonable. The median depth to water is about 30 feet, with the middle half of measurements between 13 and 60 feet below the surface. That’s shallow enough that a typical submersible pump doesn’t have to work excessively hard, even if the well itself is a hundred feet or more deep.

Looking at medians by decade, water levels have bounced around rather than showing a clear long-term decline: about 32 feet in the 2000s, 50 feet in the 2010s, and 30 feet so far in the 2020s. That points more to climate and seasonal variability than a steady drop, but it still pays to look at the static level on the specific well you’re buying and to size your pump and storage with some margin.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling here and when
sections.html:
Jackson County’s drilling history is spread out over many decades. Permitting picked up in the 1970s with 169 wells, climbed again in the 1980s with 194, and peaked in the 1990s at 374 permits. Activity stayed solid in the 2000s with 272 permits, then eased off to 142 in the 2010s and 96 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit on record is from 2025, so new wells are still being drilled.

Stolns & Son Drilling (Stolns, Lewis B.) shows up on 213 wells, making them the most active in the records, followed by Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 95 and James Drilling (Keaton, Jordan K.) with 56. When you look at an existing well log, the driller’s name and year can tell you a lot about the construction style and what equipment might still be down the hole.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Jackson County
sections.html:
Drilling here is through fractured mountain bedrock—granite and gneiss—so most contractors charge per foot. The typical rate runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole itself in the ballpark of $6,500–$10,000 before any equipment or trenching.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, pitless adapter, trenching and electrical, a finished domestic well at that median depth usually ends up roughly in the $12,500–$22,000 range. If your site or neighbors show deeper wells in the 160-foot upper-middle range, budget proportionally higher. In fractured rock areas like this, the smart move is to plan financially for going deeper than the median, then be pleasantly surprised if you hit water sooner.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yields, contamination, and site layout
sections.html:
Even with generally good yields, Jackson County still has some risk areas. Around 2% of tested wells report under 1 gpm, and another 9% are between 1 and 5 gpm. Those wells can work with storage tanks and careful use, but they’re less forgiving for big households or livestock. It’s worth comparing any new lot to nearby well logs before you close.

There are also mapped environmental concerns in the county: 28 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 54 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those don’t automatically mean a problem on your parcel, but they are a signal to review maps, ask for water-quality test results, and plan your septic and building locations to keep good separation from the well.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Jackson County
sections.html:
For a rural homesite in Jackson County, the numbers are generally in your favor: a 100-foot median depth, 10.0 gpm median yield, and a 30-foot median static water level all point to workable domestic wells in most areas. Still, fractured-bedrock aquifers can change over a short distance, so your specific site geology and nearby well records matter.

Most wells on record are for domestic or household use, about 68%, with 23% for stock and small shares for irrigation and monitoring. That mix tells you this is established as a residential and ranching well area, not a high-volume irrigation basin. Before you buy, pull the permit and drill report, confirm the use allowed, check any nearby environmental sites, and make sure your driveway, septic, and building plan leave enough room for a compliant well location.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Jackson County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Jackson County the median well depth is about 100 feet, with the middle half of wells between 60 and 160 feet deep. About 41% of wells are under 100 feet, and 51% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Deeper wells are less common: only 7% run 300–600 feet and 1% are over 600 feet. Always check nearby well logs for your specific area before you budget.

faq.q: How much water do Jackson County wells usually produce?
faq.a: Reported yields in Jackson County are relatively strong for a mountain county. The median pump yield is 10.0 gpm, and the middle half of wells fall between 7.0 and 15.0 gpm. Only about 2% of tested wells come in under 1 gpm, and 9% are 1–5 gpm. Most, 63%, pump 5–15 gpm, with 26% at 15+ gpm. That’s plenty for a normal exempt household well when managed properly.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Jackson County, CO?
faq.a: With fractured granite and gneiss bedrock, typical drilling rates in Jackson County run about $65–$100 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, that puts the bare hole roughly in the $6,500–$10,000 range. When you include casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical, a complete domestic well at that depth often totals around $12,500–$22,000. Deeper wells in your area will push costs higher.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Jackson County wells?
faq.a: County-wide data do not show a clear long-term decline. Median static water level was about 32 feet below ground in the 2000s, shifted to 50 feet in the 2010s, and is around 30 feet in the 2020s so far. That pattern looks more like climate and measurement variability than a steady downward trend. Still, you should check the current static level on the specific well you’re buying or drilling.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Jackson County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety comes down to the individual well and its surroundings. Jackson County has 28 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 54 historic mine features, and 3 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped sites mean you should take water-quality testing seriously, especially for a new purchase. A basic lab test for bacteria and key minerals is a good starting point, with more detailed panels if you’re near known sites.
